definition.en-US: One screen of content, such as a home page, that a browser shows as a single document.

analogy.en-US: Like one sheet in a folder of printed sheets, where the whole folder stands for the website.

definition.en-US: The program that finds a web page on the internet and draws it on your screen.

analogy.en-US: Like a librarian who fetches a book from the shelves and opens it on your table.

definition.en-US: A named piece of stored data on a computer, such as a text file, from which a website is built.

analogy.en-US: Like a document saved in a labelled folder on your desk, so you can find it again later.

definition.en-US: The written request that says what to build, who it is for and how you will know it is finished.

analogy.en-US: Like the order form you give a carpenter, which says what to build and how you will check it when it is done.

definition.en-US: HyperText Markup Language, the code that gives a web page its structure, such as headings, paragraphs and links.

analogy.en-US: Like the skeleton of a house, which decides where the rooms and walls go.

definition.en-US: Cascading Style Sheets, the code that styles web content so that it looks the way you want.

analogy.en-US: Like the paint, furniture and decorations that make the same rooms feel warm or cold.

definition.en-US: A programming language that adds features and behaviour to a web page, such as reacting when someone clicks a button.

analogy.en-US: Like the electric switches in a house, which make something happen when you press them.

definition.en-US: An element that takes the reader to another page, file or address when it is activated.

analogy.en-US: Like a road sign that points to another town.

definition.en-US: The text in an image element that describes the picture and that the browser can show in its place.

analogy.en-US: Like the caption under a photo, which tells someone what the picture shows when they cannot see it.

definition.en-US: A way of designing a page so that its layout adapts to the width of the screen it is shown on.

analogy.en-US: Like a folding table that becomes bigger or smaller depending on how many people sit down.

definition.en-US: The area of the screen where a browser draws the page, which a meta tag can hint how to size.

analogy.en-US: Like the window of a shop, which decides how much of the room people can see from the street.

definition.en-US: A CSS rule that applies its styles only when a condition, such as a narrow screen, is true.

analogy.en-US: Like a rule that says the umbrella comes out only when it is raining.

definition.en-US: The algorithm that decides which CSS value applies when more than one rule sets the same property.

analogy.en-US: Like a family rule list where the most specific instruction for the situation is the one that is followed.
